About: Centrifugal Force — A Ball on a Merry-Go-Round (3D)

Source

Lecture
Classical mechanics — non-inertial frames & fictitious forces
Simulation
"The Centrifugal Force — A Ball on a Merry-Go-Round" · 3D carousel with two synchronized views (ground/inertial ↔ rotating camera, plus side-by-side), trails in both frames, counterfactual "fling" mode
Concept
The centrifugal force is not a real interaction: it appears only when motion is described in a rotating frame (Fcf = mω²r, radially outward); the ground view shows straight-line or at-rest motion under real forces only.
Serves
Frame-dependence of fictitious forces · Newton's 1st law as the ground-frame explanation · reading and scaling F = mω²r (m = 1 kg, ω = 1.5 rad/s, r = 2 m → 4.5 N outward; ω = 1, r = 1 → 1 N; F ∝ ω² and ∝ r)
Inquiry
Where is the outward force in the ground view? · How does Fcf change when ω doubles? · Which facts are identical in both frames?
Misconception
"Centrifugal force is a real outward interaction acting on the ball." Nothing exerts it; the released ball's ground-frame path is a straight tangent line, never a radial fling — the outward push exists only in the rotating description.

Centrifugal Force: Merry-Go-Round
drag to orbit, scroll to zoom

Guided Inquiry

1 · The apparatus

Let’s meet the apparatus. A carousel deck turns at a constant angular speed ω. A ball rests on the frictionless deck at radius r, held there by a backstop that turns with it. The same release can be filmed by a camera fixed to the ground, or by a camera bolted to the deck — and that choice will matter.

2 · The path after release

Let’s start with the ground camera. The deck turns at ω, and the backstop lets the ball go at radius r. Filmed from the ground, what path do you think the ball follows afterwards?

3 · Two cameras, one release

Now let’s bring in the second camera. Both cameras film the same release, so release the ball, then compare the cyan ground trail with the orange deck trail. Which features of the motion are identical in the two records, and which aren’t?

4 · The source of the outward push

Here’s the puzzle. On the deck camera, the released ball moves outward as though shoved. So which object do you think exerts that shove?

5 · Doubling the spin

Now let’s put a number on it. The ball is held at r = 2.0 m while the deck turns at ω = 1.00 rad/s. Then the deck speeds up to ω = 2.00 rad/s at the same radius. What do you think — the outward term in the deck frame becomes

6 · What makes a force fictitious

Let’s pull it all together. Every event and every real force is the same in both films; only the outward term appears or disappears with the choice of camera. A force with no source object and no reaction partner is called fictitious — here it’s mω²r, radially outward, in the deck frame alone.

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A ball sits on a spinning carousel deck, held by a backstop, and is then let go. One camera fixed to the ground and one riding on the deck film the same motion, so you can compare the two points of view.

What you'll learn

  • How the path of the released ball depends on which camera films it.
  • Which force keeps the held ball on its circle, and which way it points.
  • Where the outward "centrifugal force" comes from, and how to test whether a force is real.
  • How the size of that outward term depends on ω and r.
Seen from above: the deck turns anticlockwise at ω. The backstop holds the ball at radius r until you release it.

What's on screen

  • Cyan trail: the ball's path as the ground camera films it.
  • Orange trail: the ball's path as the deck camera films it.
  • N (backstop) arrow and label: the backstop's push while it holds the ball.
  • Fcent arrow and label: the outward term, with its size in newtons.
  • Coriolis arrow and label: the Coriolis term, when its chip in the rotating legend is on.
  • Centrifugal force readout (Controls panel): Fcent at the hold radius.
See itBoth cameras film the ball while the backstop holds it. Watch for: in the right-hand (rotating) view the deck stands still and the park turns around it.

Moving a slider or switching camera puts the ball back in the backstop. Fixed: m = 1 kg, a frictionless deck and ground.

03

One release, two films

  • Ground camera. After release nothing pushes the ball sideways: the deck is frictionless and the backstop has dropped away. So the ball keeps the velocity it had, tangent to its circle, of size v = ωr, and moves in a straight line at constant speed (Newton's first law).
  • Deck camera. The same flight, re-plotted in coordinates that turn with the deck, is an outward spiral that curls back against the spin. The ball seems to be shoved outward.
  • Nothing about the ball differs between the two films. Only the camera does.
One release at ω = 1.50 rad/s, r = 2.0 m, seen from above. Dotted: the hold circle.
The deck film is the ground film turned back by the angle the deck has turned, ωt.
See itRelease the ball with both cameras running. Watch for: on the left the trail runs off in a straight line; on the right the same flight sweeps outward in a long curve around the carousel.
04

The held ball needs an inward push

  • Ground view. Before release the ball goes round a circle, so it is accelerating toward the axis. That takes a real inward (centripetal) force of size mω²r, and the backstop supplies it: the arrow labelled N (backstop).
  • Deck view. Here the ball sits still, yet N still pushes inward. For F = ma to give zero, the deck frame adds an outward term of the same size, mω²r. That is the centrifugal force, the arrow labelled Fcent.
The held ball in the deck frame, at ω = 1.50 rad/s, r = 2.0 m.
Deck-frame balance while the ball is held.

A rider on a carousel feels the same thing: the seat or rail pushing inward. The feeling of being flung out is your body's tendency to keep going straight.

See itBoth cameras film the held ball. Watch for: the N (backstop) label shows in both views, the Fcent label only in the right-hand (rotating) view.
05

No object exerts it

To keep F = ma true in a frame turning at ω, you must add two terms to the real forces:

Newton's second law in the deck frame.
  • Centrifugal: mω²r, straight out from the axis, acting wherever the ball is.
  • Coriolis: sideways to the ball's motion, and only when the ball moves relative to the deck. It bends the path back against the spin.
  • The test for a real force is to name the object that exerts it. After release the deck is frictionless and the backstop is gone, so nothing pushes outward. These terms have no source and no reaction partner, which is why they are called fictitious. Switch to the ground camera and both vanish.
See itRelease the ball on the deck camera, with the Coriolis arrow on. Watch for: the Fcent and Coriolis labels stay with the ball after the backstop has dropped away, though nothing touches it.
06

How big it is

  • The term grows as the square of ω: double the spin and it becomes four times larger. Doubling r only doubles it.
  • It depends on where the ball is now. After release r grows, so the term grows: at the default settings it is 4.50 N at release and 7.65 N at the deck edge (r = 3.4 m).
ω r

See itHold the ball at r = 2.0 m with ω = 1.00 rad/s, then with ω = 2.00 rad/s. Watch for: the two Centrifugal force readings, side by side at the end.
See itRelease the ball on the deck camera at your settings. Watch for: the number on the Fcent label climbing as the ball moves outward.
07

Where it matters

  • The spinning Earth. We all stand on a rotating frame, turning once a day. At the equator the outward term is about 0.034 m/s², roughly 1/290 of g, so a scale reads about 0.3% less there than the same spot would without the spin. The same spin is why Earth bulges about 21 km at the equator.
  • Centrifuges. A lab ultracentrifuge at ω ≈ 3000 rad/s (about 29 000 rpm) and r = 10 cm gives ω²r ≈ 9×10⁵ m/s², about 90 000 g, enough to separate particles by size and density.
  • Spin dryers. In the ground frame, water leaves through the holes in the drum along straight tangent lines, just like the ball after release.
The outward term at Earth's equator.
Go deeper: one point in both films
  • Take the defaults (ω = 1.50 rad/s, r = 2.0 m), start the clock at release, and put the release point on the x axis, with y pointing the way the deck turns.
  • At t = 0.5 s the ground film has the ball at (2.00, 1.50) m. The deck has turned 0.75 rad (43°). Turning the point back by that angle gives (2.49, −0.27) m in the deck film.
  • So in the deck film the ball is already at r = 2.50 m, outside its hold circle, and behind the spoke it was released from.
08

Summary

In one line. The centrifugal force, mω²r outward, is a term you add to keep F = ma working in a rotating frame. No object exerts it, and in the ground frame it does not exist.

Key points

  • Released, the ball moves in a straight tangent line in the ground frame, and in an outward spiral in the deck frame.
  • While held, the backstop's real inward push keeps the ball on its circle. In the deck frame the outward term balances it.
  • The term is mω²r: four times larger for twice the spin, twice as large for twice the radius.

Common mix-ups

  • "Released, the ball flies straight out along the spoke." It leaves along the tangent. A radial path would need an outward force, and there is none.
  • "Centrifugal and centripetal force are an action–reaction pair." Both act on the same ball. The real pair is the backstop pushing the ball and the ball pushing back on the backstop.
  • "If you feel flung outward, an outward force must be acting." What you feel is the seat pushing you inward.

Things to try on your own

  • Set ω = 0 and release the ball. Compare the two views.
  • Set r = 1.0 m and then r = 3.0 m at the same ω, and compare the Centrifugal force readings.
  • Release the ball on the Rotating camera with the Coriolis arrow on, and note which way the Coriolis arrow points.
